Close every gap identified in the 2026-06-10 docs/v2-vs-implementation audit (the
first audit run *after* drift-remediation Waves 1–4) so that: (1) docs/v2 makes no
shipped-claim about unshipped behavior, (2) every security/integrity step the
design requires is **deterministic code on the real path, not model prose**,

(5) max-autonomy is a documented recipe with a `qa` PASS-only token, and
(6) the operator's dashboard vision ships: `/guild:dashboard` launches the

# Observability, Tracing & Replay

**Guild is explainable after the fact.** A human (or the benchmark) can reconstruct what Guild
did, which agent did it, what context that agent saw, which tools ran, what changed, and why
the workflow chose its path. The backbone is **one canonical trace** plus a **run-lifecycle
contract** that bookends every run with a start manifest and a close-shape provenance record —
all filesystem-canonical.

The boundary that makes this work is the **telemetry split**: the **plugin records, the
benchmark analyzes**. The plugin owns and emits the on-disk format; the benchmark reads it by
format. Neither repo imports the other — the plugin must build and run with the benchmark
absent.

## The canonical trace

| Sink | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Canonical trace (frozen) | `.guild/runs/<run-id>/logs/v1.4-events.jsonl` | one JSON object/line; the **plugin↔benchmark contract boundary** |
| Legacy telemetry mirror | `.guild/runs/<run-id>/events.ndjson` | legacy compatibility mirror only; never the primary |

The trace event is **FROZEN** as `guild.trace_event.v1`; bind by pointer, never re-spell the
field names or the `schema_version` string. Canonical body:
[`data-model.md`](..<HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED>-model.md).

`guild.trace_event.v2` is an **additive, backward-compatible successor** (lenient reader) — it
preserves the v1 field set **verbatim and frozen** and adds optional `span_id`,
`parent_span_id`, `tier`, `model`, and a `tokens` block (`input`/`output`/`cached`/`cost_usd`)
present only on LLM-call events. `span_id` is generated deterministically at write time by the
hook; `parent_span_id` is set by the orchestrator and threaded via `GUILD_PARENT_SPAN_ID`
(`null` = root span). The `.v2` bump is the forward-compat lever the v1 spec reserved; old v1
traces stay queryable by any v2 reader. Canonical body:
[`v2-observability-and-replay.md §D-OBS-1`](..<HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED>-observability-and-replay.md).

A structured **redacted payload sidecar** (`guild.trace_payload.v1`) at
`<runDir>/logs/payloads/<evt-id>.json` stores field-name-preserved, secret-masked bodies for
tool calls and specialist inputs — kept out of the main JSONL so the event log stays
streamable. **Raw provider prompts are never stored**; redaction is path-category-only for
secrets.

## The run-lifecycle contract

Every run is bookended by two sibling records — never merged:

| Record | `schema_version` | Written | Path |
|---|---|---|---|
| Start manifest | `guild.run.v1` | once at run-start by `startRun()` | `.guild/runs/<run-id>/run.yaml` |
| Close-shape provenance | `guild.provenance.v1` | once at run-close by `closeRun()` | `.gui... [TRUNCATED]

# Dispatch & Execution

**Every unit of Guild work is dispatched through one neutral contract and routed
along three orthogonal axes.** A `task_run` describes *what* must happen; the

# Config & Command Surfaces

**Guild has exactly one config file and one command grammar.** All behavior lives
in `.guild/settings.json` — a single JSON file under a closed-key reject regime,
resolved through a 7-source inheritance chain where **CLI flags always win**. All
user input is a flat-token command `/guild:<verb>` — six phase verbs plus a small
set of nouns and maintenance verbs, with **five global flags + `--dry-run`** for
the tuning surface. Skills are **model-invoked, never typed**.

This is the operator's control surface: what you type, what you set, and how the
two compose. The lifecycle the verbs drive is defined in
[`lifecycle`](lifecycle.md); the dispatch keys' *semantics* are in
[`dispatch-execution`](dispatch-execution.md); this doc owns the **surface**
— the file, the grammar, and the flags.

## 1. `.guild/settings.json` — the single config surface

There is **ONE config file**: `.guild/settings.json` (JSON). It replaces the v1
`.guild/config.yml` (YAML); the `config.yml` runtime reader is **removed in v2.0**
(convert a v1 file with `/guild:migrate`). JSON has no comments, so the scaffold
embeds a top-level `"_help"` block (keys prefixed `_` are reader-ignored
annotations).

**Closed-key reject regime.** Config is human-authored, so a typo must surface —
the reader is **not** lenient here (unlike the frozen `guild.*.v1` artifact
contracts). Unknown keys are **rejected at Session Intake / `--validate`**, not
silently ignored. Three rejections are absolute:

| Rule | Rejected | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Unknown key | any key/sub-key outside the closed set | typos must surface |
| `defaults.wiki.autopromote: true` | always rejected | agents emit knowledge **candidates only** — never auto-promote |
| `defaults.adversarial: off` | rejected for Guild self-build | self-build keeps adversarial review always-on |

**Authoring surface.** `/guild:config <init|show|validate|set|providers>`:
- `config init` scaffolds `settings.json` with every key = default + the `_help`
  block (idempotent — never clobbers operator config); `/guild:init` scaffolds it
  at bootstrap if absent.
- `config show` prints the resolved config; `config show --sources` annotates
  each key with the inheritance layer that won it.
- `config validate` runs the closed-key checks on the raw file; `--effective`
  validates the post-inheritance resolved config.
- `config set <key> <value> --scope workspace|project|local` performs a scoped,
  read-modify-write **hard-set** (always-asks under auto-approve; never clobbers
  unrelated keys or `_help`; validates every dotted segment against the closed
  set before writing).
- `config providers detect` probes the available cross-review providers
  (`codex-plugin`, `codex-cli`, and detect-only `gemini-cli`/`pi`/`antigravity`)
  and prints a detection table — the operator-facing companion to the
  host/adversarial reso... [TRUNCATED]

## `guild.trace_event.v2` Schema Extension

Additive-only extension of `guild.trace_event.v1`. Backward-compatible: lenient readers
on old traces ignore unknown fields. The frozen v1 field set is never modified.

New fields added in v2:

```jsonc
{
  // --- existing v1 fields preserved verbatim ---
  "schema_version": "guild.trace_event.v2",
  "id": "evt_001",
  "run_id": "...",
  "task_run_id": "...",
  "timestamp": "<iso8601>",
  "event_type": "...",
  "actor_type": "...",
  "actor_id": "...",
  "host": "...",
  "payload_ref": "...",
  "status": "...",
  "redaction": "...",

  // --- v2 additions ---
  "span_id": "span_abc",          // stable per-event ID for span-tree reconstruction
  "parent_span_id": null,         // links child events to parent span (null = root)
  "tier": "cheap|mid|powerful",   // resolved tier for this event's actor
  "model": "haiku|sonnet|opus",   // concrete model name
  "tokens": {                     // ONLY when event represents an LLM call
    "input": 1024,
    "output": 312,
    "cached": 800,
    "cost_usd": 0.0014
  }
}
```

`span_id` generation: `sha256(run_id + "|" + event_type + "|" + timestamp + "|" + actor_id).slice(0, 16)`,
generated by the hook script at write time. `parent_span_id` is set by the orchestrator
layer and threaded via `GUILD_PARENT_SPAN_ID` env var (mirrors existing `GUILD_RUN_ID`
and `GUILD_LANE_ID` threading).
[source: `.<HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED>-replay.md §5`, ADR-OBS-6]

Where an advisory panel exists (Quality, Operations) it is **distinct from** this
gate-level cross-host broker review (`docs/v2/adversarial-review.md §Loop control`) — the two
compose, they do not replace one another. **G-init has no advisory panel** — its
review is the cross-host broker gate alone. This table is the broker-side gate
registry; each gate's actual review shape is as shown.

## Gate-pass rule (checksum-bound, SK-9)

The broker writes the AC-9 `review/<gate>/` packet/result/trail set (above);
**this section adds the integrity binding** that makes the gate-pass
checksum-bound (`docs/v2/adversarial-review.md §Gate-pass rule`). The result binds to the reviewed
artifact by **SHA-256**, computed over the artifact bytes **after
secret-scrubbing** (the same SHA-256 that serves as the cross-host cache key on
the artifact bus).

A gate **passes iff all five conditions hold**:

1. the `review_result` **parses** as `review_result.v1`, AND
2. `result.packet_id` **matches** the packet id the broker issued for the round, AND
3. `result.artifact_sha256_reviewed == sha256(current artifact bytes)` (recomputed
   now, post-scrub), AND
4. (`result.verdict == "satisfied"`) **OR** a human **`force_pass`**, AND
5. **no blocking findings remain** (`blocking_findings` empty).

`status: "skipped"` passes the gate **only** when `review_required == false` (the
policy did not require review). It is **never** an up-conversion of a
`degraded-local` / cap-hit / unsatisfied result — those are exactly what they say
(`docs/v2/adversarial-review.md §AC-8`).

**Artifact-changed-mid-review → reject + restart.** If the artifact's bytes
changed during the round, condition 3 fails (the recomputed SHA-256 will not
match `artifact_sha256_reviewed`): **reject the result and restart the round**
against the new bytes — do not pass a verdict that critiqued stale content. This
is the same checksum-mismatch rule the sentinel-hardening table enforces.

**The weak path obeys the identical rule.** A same-host fresh-context review
(other host unavailable) is stamped `independence: weak` and recorded, but it
passes the gate **only** by satisfying the same five conditions — weak
independence relaxes *who* may review, never *whether* the checksum/blocker gate
holds.

Compute the SHA-256 with `sha256(<scrubbed-artifact-bytes>)`; the broker records
both `artifact_sha256_reviewed` (from the result) and the recomputed current
hash in the trail so a reviewer-vs-current mismatch is auditable.

## Input shape

```typescript
type ReviewBrokerInput = {
  gate: "G-init" | "G-spec" | "G-plan" | "G-quality" | "G-operations" | "G-diagnose" | `G-lane:${string}`;

{"stdout":"## Transport — v2.0 is filesystem-canonical, co-located

Both hosts run on the **same filesystem**. The broker speaks to the reviewer
host purely through files under `.guild/runs/<run-id>/review/<gate>/`:

1. The broker writes a **review packet** — the artifact + adversarial
   instructions + (rounds 2+) the prior round trail.
2. The reviewer host reads the packet from the shared filesystem.
3. The reviewer host writes back a **`review_result.v1`** JSON envelope.
4. The broker reads the result, checks the verdict, and loops or terminates.

The cross-host **dispatch + packet/result FS contract** is owned by the
transport layer **RE-4 / RE-5** (built this wave by impl-runtime-backend) —
**bind by pointer, do not re-implement here.** This skill owns the *broker
logic* (author/reviewer resolution, the round loop, sentinel detection,
escalation); RE-4/RE-5 own *how the packet reaches the reviewer and the result
comes back*. Where a remote transport is NOT CONFIGURED (cross_host disabled /

A **remote** reviewer host — one on another machine pulling the packet over

Guild supports three execution backends. |---|---|---|
| **Agent teams (tmux panes)** | `team` — `auto` + tmux available (the common case on a dev machine) **or** an explicit `team` pin. # Command Reference

All Guild commands follow the flat `/guild:<verb>` pattern. The main entry point is `/guild:guild [brief]` — it runs the full lifecycle from whatever phase your project is currently at.

![Guild's 14 specialists across engineering, content, and commercial groups — each /guild command dispatches into this team roster](<HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED>-teams.svg)

The `:` plugin namespace is a Claude Code requirement and stays in v2; the redundant `guild-` prefix from v1 is dropped (e.g., `/guild:guild-wiki` → `/guild:wiki`). Sub-verbs (`wiki ingest`, `config init`, `learn map`) are **positional arguments** to the command, never separate command files or nested namespaces.

Skills (`guild:brainstorm`, `guild:plan`, etc.) are **model-invoked, never typed** by the user. The command `/guild:<token>` and the skill `guild:<token>` share a stem but are distinct surfaces.

---

## Main lifecycle command

| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `/guild:guild [brief]` | Run the full lifecycle from the current phase. Proposes a phase and asks before proceeding — never silent. Accepts an optional brief as a quoted string. |

**Phase detection:** bare `/guild:guild` surfaces a phase-detection prompt. To start at
a specific phase, use a phase subcommand (see below) or pass `--rigor=quick|standard|deep`.

---

## Phase subcommands

Each phase command is a thin entrypoint that invokes its skill(s) in order. See the
[phase-to-skill dispatch table](#phase-to-skill-dispatch) for the exact skill chain.

| Command | Phase | What it does |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| `/guild:init` | Init | Bootstrap the project wiki, CodebaseMap stub, and architecture-map. The `learn-*` subset (`learn-map` → `learn-graph` → `learn-onboard`) runs only under `--learn` or `defaults.auto_learn: true`. |
| `/guild:ideate` | Ideation | Generate the spec. With `--rigor=deep`, wraps in `guild:loop-clarify`. |
| `/guild:plan` | Planning | Compose the team and write the plan. With `--rigor=deep`, + `guild:loop-plan-review`. Team composition is a sub-step here (not a separate command). |
| `/guild:build` | Development | Execute per-lane: context-assemble → execute-plan → review. With `--rigor=deep`, + `guild:loop-implement`. |
| `/guild:qa` | Quality | Run the full `guild:quality` skill — auto-selects and executes <HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED> checks from CodebaseMap + plan signals. |
| `/guild:ops` | Operations | Run the full `guild:operations` skill — executes <HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED> runbooks under a split autonomy posture with four safety rails. |

---

## Learn command

| Command | Sub-verb | What it does |
|---------|----------|-------------|
| `/guild:learn` | (none) | Smart full learn-all: detects target shape, runs the full learn pipeline, updates indexes, emits knowledge candidates. Sub-verbs are optional refinements. |
| `/guild:learn map` | `map` | Build a brownfield CodebaseMap. |
| `/guild:learn graph` | `graph` | Build the deep knowledge-graph. |
| `/guild:learn onboard` | `onboard` | Generate an onboarding document for new contributors. |
| `/guild:learn diff` | `diff` | Explain recent changes from the git diff. |
| `/guild:learn explain` | `explain` | Explain a specified component or file in depth. |

`/guild:learn` shares **one implementation** with `/guild:init --learn` (and
`defaults.auto_learn`), but the entry points differ in scope: Init calls a subset —
`learn-map` → `learn-graph` → `learn-onboard` (it skips `diff`/`explain`) — while no-arg

# guild:audit

Implements `guild-plan.md §15.1 #12` (privacy + egress — meta-skills restricted to filesystem; only researcher has web access by default; `/guild:audit` surfaces script hashes) and the `§15.2` "Arbitrary code in installed skills" risk (the plugin is only as safe as its installed-from source — install from trusted sources per Anthropic's guidance).

The audit is **static** — it reads source files, computes hashes, greps for egress and filesystem patterns, and writes a dated report. It does not execute any script under audit.

## Scope

Audits every executable artifact that ships in the plugin:

- `hooks/*.ts` and `hooks/*.sh` — SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse, SubagentStop, Stop hooks per `§13.2`.
- `hooks/agent-team/*.ts` — `TaskCreated`, `TaskCompleted`, `TeammateIdle` hooks per `§13.2`.
- `scripts/*.ts` — tooling scripts (trace-summarize, evolve-loop, flip-report, shadow-mode, description-optimizer, rollback-walker, and any others added in P7+).
- `mcp-servers/*` — optional MCP servers per `§13.3` (`guild-memory`, `guild-telemetry`), audited if present.

Does **not** audit:

- `skills/**/SKILL.md` — markdown, no executable code. Skill bodies are instructions to the model, not programs; they are audited by the `guild:evolve-skill` gate and the `guild:wiki-lint` skill for content, not by this skill for egress.
- `agents/*.md` — same rationale.
- `commands/*.md` — same.
- user application code — that's `agents/security` (the shipping specialist), not this skill.

# Configuration Reference

Guild works without any configuration. `.guild/settings.json` exists only when you want to override a default — absent keys fall back to the built-in defaults. Unknown keys in the `defaults.*` and `models.*` blocks are rejected by the explicit `config validate` command (non-zero exit); the run-start resolver, by contrast, silently drops unknown keys from the effective config rather than failing the run.

```bash
/guild:config init      # scaffold settings.json with all keys + _help block
/guild:config show --sources   # show every resolved key annotated with its source layer
/guild:config validate --effective   # validate the effective resolved config
/guild:config set <key> <value> --scope workspace|project|local   # write one key at a scope
/guild:config providers detect   # probe cross-review providers; print detection table
```

---

## Settings inheritance chain

Guild resolves settings through a **7-source chain** (least to most authoritative):

```
built-in defaults
  < workspace .guild/settings.json
  < workspace .guild/settings.local.json   (gitignored; machine-local overrides)
  < project   .guild/settings.json
  < project   .guild/settings.local.json   (gitignored)
  < --rigor profile expansion
  < CLI flags
```

In a workspace layout (monorepo root with child projects), workspace settings propagate to every child project automatically. A child project that sets only some keys overrides just those keys; the rest inherit from the workspace root. Deep-merge applies to nested blocks — a child that sets `defaults.team.size` does not discard the workspace-level `defaults.quality.budget`.

**Non-inheritable keys.** Two keys have restricted workspace→child propagation:

- `workspace.mode` — workspace detection applies only to the root. A child never inherits the root's workspace classification (unconditional).
- `initiative_default` — inherits workspace→child **only when the workspace's `initiative_default` names an initiative that is `scope:workspace`**. Otherwise a child resolves its own `initiative_default` or falls back to the built-in `null` — this prevents child runs from being silently attached to a project-scoped parent initiative.

All other keys inherit.

**`config show --sources`** renders every resolved key labeled with the layer that won: `builtin | workspace | workspace-local | project | project-local | rigor | cli`.

**`config set <key> <value> --scope <scope>`** writes to the correct layer file using dotted key-path resolution. It never clobbers unrelated keys or `_help` annotations, and throws on malformed JSON rather than overwriting. `--scope workspace` is a HARD-SET write (always prompts under auto-approve).

**`config validate`** (raw, on a single settings file) runs the closed-key reject rules — unknown `defaults.*` and `models.*` keys fail non-zero. **`config validate --effective`** validates the fully *resolved* config instead; because resolution silently drops unknown keys, `--effective` checks the merged result's known keys rather than catching unknowns (use raw `config validate` for that).

**`config providers detect`** prints a read-only detection table of all known cross-review providers, including which provider would be recommended for `review=cross`. READ-ONLY — no settings file is written. Also runs automatically at run-start preflight. The shipped `config` subcommands are `init`, `set`, `show`, `validate`, and `providers detect`.

## What changed from the first submission (Codex G-lane fixes)

### MAJOR fix — probe-fixture removed from production CLI

The `--probe-fixture` flag has been completely removed from `parseArgs`,
`ParsedArgs`, and the production CLI. There is no longer any file-read hook
reachable from the CLI.

`cmdProvidersDetect` now has this signature:

```typescript
export function cmdProvidersDetect(cwd: string, probe?: ProbeEnv): number
```

The `probe` parameter is an optional `ProbeEnv` (the injectable seam from
`provider-detect.ts`). When absent, the function falls back to
`defaultProbeEnv(cwd)` — the real shelling probe. The production CLI dispatch
in `main()` calls `cmdProvidersDetect(parsed.cwd)` with no probe.

Tests import `cmdProvidersDetect` directly and pass a deterministic fake
`ProbeEnv` — no file I/O, no CLI flag, no path-read hook anywhere in production.

`loadProbeFixture()` has been deleted entirely.

### Additional fix — `main()` guarded against import-time execution

# codex-review-user-facing-opt-in
## Context
Codex adversarial review started as a development discipline for Guild's own
plugin work. `/guild:diagnose` and the broader loop work made it useful as an
operator-requested second opinion, but making it default would add cost and
availability risk.

## Options considered
- Keep Codex review dev-only and undocumented for users.
- Enable Codex review by default on all `/guild` runs.
- Expose it as an explicit `--codex-review` opt-in with graceful skip.

## Decision
Promote adversarial review to a documented opt-in feature via `--review=cross` (v2;
v1 flag was `--codex-review`, replaced at v2) - because users should be able to
request cross-host review when the stakes justify it, while default Guild runs
stay independent of Codex availability and cost.

## Consequences
Codex review trails are durable under `.guild/runs/<run-id>/codex-review/*.md`.
The feature must skip cleanly when Codex is unavailable, and schema support must
cover every documented gate. The `--codex-review` flag is superseded by
`--review=local|cross|off` (see `<HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED>-surface.md §D`).

# Cost-Aware Model Tiering

Every specialist lane runs on the cheapest model that can handle the work — file reads and summarization on haiku, drafting and reasoning on sonnet, architecture and security review on opus. Guild scores each lane automatically before dispatch and prints the resolved tier so you can see exactly what ran and why.

<Figure src="/diagrams/cost-tiering.svg" alt="Three-tier model diagram: cheap (haiku) for I/O and classification, mid (sonnet) for drafting and reasoning, powerful (opus) for architecture and security" caption="Guild routes each lane to the right tier. You only pay opus rates when the stakes justify it." />

## The three tiers

| Tier | Default model | Typical work |
|---|---|---|
| `cheap` | haiku | File read, tokenize, chunk, summarize, classify, tag — pure I/O, template-guided, low ambiguity |
| `mid` | sonnet | Draft, reason, plan subtasks, single-doc + cross-file relationship extraction — **default task-agent tier** |
| `powerful` | opus | Architecture decisions, security review, graph schema/topology, advisor/critic passes — high-stakes, low frequency |

The tier-to-model map is **host-agnostic**: it lives in `settings.json` under `models.tiers` as `{ cheap, mid, powerful } → { claude, codex, gemini }`. Codex and Gemini slots are `null` by default; adding a new host is a config edit plus an adapter.

## Auto-scoring a lane

For each lane, the orchestrator computes a complexity score from deterministic signals — no LLM call, no guesswork:

| Signal | Score contribution |
|---|---|
| `workType` verb: read/summarize | 0 |
| `workType` verb: draft/extract | +1 |
| `workType` verb: <HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED> | +2 |
| Blast-radius — affected file/module count (each unit ≥1) | + count × `scoreWeights.blastRadius` |
| Upstream `depends-on:` contract present | +1 |
| <HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED> sensitivity flag | +1 |
| Prior-attempt escalation on this lane | +1 (sticky for the run) |

Score bands map to tiers:

| Score | Tier |
|---|---|
| 0 | `cheap` |
| 1–2 | `mid` |
| ≥ 3 | `powerful` |

Score and resolved tier are printed at dispatch. Signal weights are tunable via `models.scoreWeights` in `settings.json`.

## Precedence

```
--model-tier=<tier>   CLI flag           (top — run-level escape hatch)
  > tier: <tier> in plan lane            (per-lane override in .guild/plan/*.md)
    > settings.json models:              (repo config)
      > built-in default                 (cheap-biased tier-map)
```

Use `--model-tier` only as a one-off override. Permanent adjustments belong in `settings.json` or the plan lane. See the [configuration reference](/docs/configuration) for all `models.*` keys.

## Advisor escalation

When a `cheap` or `mid` specialist hits a sub-question above its tier — something ambiguous enough that guessing would be wrong — it gets **one** `powerful` sub-answer for that specific question. The original specialist continues with the answer folded in. No wholesale re-run on the expensive model.

**Three triggers for advisor escalation:**

1. **Explicit signal** — the specialist emits `status: "escalate"` plus an `escalate_reason` in its `guild.handoff.v2` envelope.
2. **Uncertainty markers** — the orchestrator detects uncertainty phrases in the output (e.g., "I'm not sure", "unclear", "cannot determine") matching the `models.escalationMarkers` list.

# How Guild Works

Guild runs your task through six lifecycle phases — Init, Ideation, Planning, Development, Quality, and Operations (commands `init`, `ideate`, `plan`, `build`, `qa`, `ops`) — plus a cross-phase Reflection step. Three mandatory gates govern the planning phases: you approve the **spec**, the **team**, and the **plan** before anyone writes code. After that the run proceeds with minimal interruption — with two exceptions covered below. When it finishes, Guild proposes skill improvements and memory updates for your review; nothing auto-promotes.

This page is the user-facing walkthrough. If you haven't installed Guild yet, see [Get Started with Guild](/docs/getting-started). For the runtime internals — execution backends, hooks, security posture — see [Architecture & Lifecycle](/docs/architecture).

<Figure src="/diagrams/lifecycle.svg" alt="Guild's lifecycle: init → ideate → plan → build → qa → ops, with reflection across phases" caption="Three mandatory gates govern planning (spec, team, plan); the later phases proceed with minimal interruption — but destructive operations and --rigor=deep runs add their own gates." />

## The phase pipeline

```
/guild:guild [brief]
  ↓
init          → .guild/init/<slug>.md, wiki stubs, codebase-map.json
  ↓
ideate        → .guild/spec/<slug>.md              [gate: you approve spec]
  ↓
plan          → .guild/team/<slug>.yaml             [gate: you approve team]
              → .guild/plan/<slug>.md               [gate: you approve plan]
  ↓
build         → .guild/context/<run-id>/            (one bundle per specialist)
              → handoff receipts, assumptions.md, review.md
  ↓
qa            → .guild/runs/<run-id>/quality/
  ↓
ops           → .guild/runs/<run-id>/ops/
  ↓
reflect       → .guild/reflections/<run-id>.md      (proposals only — nothing auto-promotes)
```

## The gates

Three **mandatory interactive gates** govern the planning phases. You can't skip past them:

| Gate | When | What you approve |
|---|---|---|
| **Spec** (G-spec) | End of Ideation | The task specification — goal, scope, success criteria |
| **Team** (G-team) | During Planning | Which specialists Guild will dispatch |
| **Plan** (G-plan) | End of Planning | The per-specialist lane plan and sequencing |

Two more gate classes fire beyond those three — so "three gates, then it's hands-off" is the common case, not the whole story:

- **Destructive or network operations always prompt inline.** Any step that deletes data, writes outside `.guild/`, or makes a network call asks first — regardless of any auto-approve setting. This hard rule is unconditional.
- **`--rigor=deep` adds review loops.** Running with `--rigor=deep` turns on the L1 clarify loop in Ideation, the L2 plan-review loop in Planning, and per-lane review loops in Development. These are opt-in and add their own interaction points.

The Quality and Operations phases each carry their own gates too (a release/blocker decision in `qa`, and safety gates in `ops` — incident and rollback runbooks are never autonomous). See [Architecture & Lifecycle](/docs/architecture) for the full gate model.

## Phase-by-phase

**What you get:** A lightweight context map of your project — wiki stubs, a `codebase-map.json` summary, and an `architecture-map.md` stub. Run once per project; re-run when the codebase changes significantly. The full knowledge-graph pipeline runs only under `--learn`.

# Command Reference

All Guild commands follow the flat `/guild:<verb>` pattern. The main entry point is `/guild:guild [brief]` — it runs the full lifecycle from whatever phase your project is currently at.

![Guild's 14 specialists across engineering, content, and commercial groups — each /guild command dispatches into this team roster](<HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED>-teams.svg)

The `:` plugin namespace is a Claude Code requirement and stays in v2; the redundant `guild-` prefix from v1 is dropped (e.g., `/guild:guild-wiki` → `/guild:wiki`). Sub-verbs (`wiki ingest`, `config init`, `learn map`) are **positional arguments** to the command, never separate command files or nested namespaces.

Skills (`guild:brainstorm`, `guild:plan`, etc.) are **model-invoked, never typed** by the user. The command `/guild:<token>` and the skill `guild:<token>` share a stem but are distinct surfaces.

---

## Main lifecycle command

| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `/guild:guild [brief]` | Run the full lifecycle from the current phase. Proposes a phase and asks before proceeding — never silent. Accepts an optional brief as a quoted string. |

**Phase detection:** bare `/guild:guild` surfaces a phase-detection prompt. To start at
a specific phase, use a phase subcommand (see below) or pass `--rigor=quick|standard|deep`.

---

## Phase subcommands

Each phase command is a thin entrypoint that invokes its skill(s) in order. See the
[phase-to-skill dispatch table](#phase-to-skill-dispatch) for the exact skill chain.

| Command | Phase | What it does |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| `/guild:init` | Init | Bootstrap the project wiki, CodebaseMap stub, and architecture-map. The `learn-*` subset (`learn-map` → `learn-graph` → `learn-onboard`) runs only under `--learn` or `defaults.auto_learn: true`. |
| `/guild:ideate` | Ideation | Generate the spec. With `--rigor=deep`, wraps in `guild:loop-clarify`. |
| `/guild:plan` | Planning | Compose the team and write the plan. With `--rigor=deep`, + `guild:loop-plan-review`. Team composition is a sub-step here (not a separate command). |
| `/guild:build` | Development | Execute per-lane: context-assemble → execute-plan → review. With `--rigor=deep`, + `guild:loop-implement`. |
| `/guild:qa` | Quality | Run the full `guild:quality` skill — auto-selects and executes <HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED> checks from CodebaseMap + plan signals. |
| `/guild:ops` | Operations | Run the full `guild:operations` skill — executes <HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED> runbooks under a split autonomy posture with four safety rails. |

# Command Reference

All Guild commands follow the flat `/guild:<verb>` pattern. The main entry point is `/guild:guild [brief]` — it runs the full lifecycle from whatever phase your project is currently at.

![Guild's 14 specialists across engineering, content, and commercial groups — each /guild command dispatches into this team roster](<HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED>-teams.svg)

The `:` plugin namespace is a Claude Code requirement and stays in v2; the redundant `guild-` prefix from v1 is dropped (e.g., `/guild:guild-wiki` → `/guild:wiki`). Sub-verbs (`wiki ingest`, `config init`, `learn map`) are **positional arguments** to the command, never separate command files or nested namespaces.

Skills (`guild:brainstorm`, `guild:plan`, etc.) are **model-invoked, never typed** by the user. The command `/guild:<token>` and the skill `guild:<token>` share a stem but are distinct surfaces.

---

## Main lifecycle command

| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `/guild:guild [brief]` | Run the full lifecycle from the current phase. Proposes a phase and asks before proceeding — never silent. Accepts an optional brief as a quoted string. |

**Phase detection:** bare `/guild:guild` surfaces a phase-detection prompt. To start at
a specific phase, use a phase subcommand (see below) or pass `--rigor=quick|standard|deep`.

---

## Phase subcommands

Each phase command is a thin entrypoint that invokes its skill(s) in order. See the
[phase-to-skill dispatch table](#phase-to-skill-dispatch) for the exact skill chain.

| Command | Phase | What it does |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| `/guild:init` | Init | Bootstrap the project wiki, CodebaseMap stub, and architecture-map. The `learn-*` subset (`learn-map` → `learn-graph` → `learn-onboard`) runs only under `--learn` or `defaults.auto_learn: true`. |
| `/guild:ideate` | Ideation | Generate the spec. With `--rigor=deep`, wraps in `guild:loop-clarify`. |
| `/guild:plan` | Planning | Compose the team and write the plan. With `--rigor=deep`, + `guild:loop-plan-review`. Team composition is a sub-step here (not a separate command). |
| `/guild:build` | Development | Execute per-lane: context-assemble → execute-plan → review. With `--rigor=deep`, + `guild:loop-implement`. |
| `/guild:qa` | Quality | Run the full `guild:quality` skill — auto-selects and executes <HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED> checks from CodebaseMap + plan signals. |
| `/guild:ops` | Operations | Run the full `guild:operations` skill — executes <HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED> runbooks under a split autonomy posture with four safety rails. |

## Running Guild hands-off

The maximum-autonomy recipe:

```bash
/guild:guild "<brief>" --auto-approve=all --rigor=standard
```

Add `--review=cross` if you want the Claude↔Codex adversarial review gates running while you're away — they self-loop without prompting you (up to `codex_cap` rounds).

`--auto-approve` collapses the **soft** approval gates. Each token clears one pause; `all` clears them all:

| Token | What it auto-clears |
|-------|---------------------|
| `spec` | The spec approval pause (G-spec) at the end of Ideation. |
| `plan` | The team and plan approval pauses (G-team, G-plan) at the end of Planning. |
| `build` | The per-lane proceed pauses during Development. |
| `qa` | The Quality release gate — **only when the computed ReleaseGate verdict is PASS**. A BLOCK verdict always stops and asks; overriding a BLOCK is never autonomous. |
| `all` | All of the above. |

### What STILL interrupts

Soft gates are the only thing `--auto-approve` touches. These prompts fire regardless — even under `--auto-approve=all`:

| Interrupt | Why it always prompts |
|-----------|----------------------|
| Destructive, network, or spend tool calls | The always-ask hard set is unconditional. Anything that deletes data, writes outside `.guild/`, makes a non-localhost network call, or costs money asks first. |
| Quality BLOCK-override | Releasing past a computed `BLOCK` verdict is a human decision, never a soft gate. The `qa` token only auto-proceeds on PASS. |
| Operations runbook rails | All four safety rails hold: incident and rollback runbooks are **never** autonomous; the **first** ops run of any runbook class is always interactive; the always-ask hard set applies inside runbooks too; the pre-flight dry-run is mandatory. There is no `ops` auto-approve token — by design. |
| `--install` network actions | Commands that fetch from the network on your behalf (e.g. the [dashboard launcher](/docs/dashboard)'s `git clone` + `npm install`) require an explicit `--install` flag or an interactive confirmation. |

Honest framing: full autonomy covers **Ideation → Quality on a green path** — spec, plan, build, and a PASS-ing release gate proceed without you. Operations stays supervised by design: anything that touches production, deletes data, or spends money keeps a human in the loop no matter what you auto-approve.

# Configuration Reference

Guild works without any configuration. `.guild/settings.json` exists only when you want to override a default — absent keys fall back to the built-in defaults. Unknown keys in the `defaults.*` and `models.*` blocks are rejected by the explicit `config validate` command (non-zero exit); the run-start resolver, by contrast, silently drops unknown keys from the effective config rather than failing the run.

```bash
/guild:config init      # scaffold settings.json with all keys + _help block
/guild:config show --sources   # show every resolved key annotated with its source layer
/guild:config validate --effective   # validate the effective resolved config
/guild:config set <key> <value> --scope workspace|project|local   # write one key at a scope
/guild:config providers detect   # probe cross-review providers; print detection table
```

---

## Settings inheritance chain

Guild resolves settings through a **7-source chain** (least to most authoritative):

```
built-in defaults
  < workspace .guild/settings.json
  < workspace .guild/settings.local.json   (gitignored; machine-local overrides)
  < project   .guild/settings.json
  < project   .guild/settings.local.json   (gitignored)
  < --rigor profile expansion
  < CLI flags
```

In a workspace layout (monorepo root with child projects), workspace settings propagate to every child project automatically. A child project that sets only some keys overrides just those keys; the rest inherit from the workspace root. Deep-merge applies to nested blocks — a child that sets `defaults.team.size` does not discard the workspace-level `defaults.quality.budget`.

**Non-inheritable keys.** Two keys have restricted workspace→child propagation:

- `workspace.mode` — workspace detection applies only to the root. A child never inherits the root's workspace classification (unconditional).
- `initiative_default` — inherits workspace→child **only when the workspace's `initiative_default` names an initiative that is `scope:workspace`**. Otherwise a child resolves its own `initiative_default` or falls back to the built-in `null` — this prevents child runs from being silently attached to a project-scoped parent initiative.

All other keys inherit.

**`config show --sources`** renders every resolved key labeled with the layer that won: `builtin | workspace | workspace-local | project | project-local | rigor | cli`.

**`config set <key> <value> --scope <scope>`** writes to the correct layer file using dotted key-path resolution. It never clobbers unrelated keys or `_help` annotations, and throws on malformed JSON rather than overwriting. `--scope workspace` is a HARD-SET write (always prompts under auto-approve).

**`config validate`** (raw, on a single settings file) runs the closed-key reject rules — unknown `defaults.*` and `models.*` keys fail non-zero. **`config validate --effective`** validates the fully *resolved* config... [TRUNCATED]

# Configuration Reference

Guild works without any configuration. `.guild/settings.json` exists only when you want to override a default — absent keys fall back to the built-in defaults. Unknown keys in the `defaults.*` and `models.*` blocks are rejected by the explicit `config validate` command (non-zero exit); the run-start resolver, by contrast, silently drops unknown keys from the effective config rather than failing the run.

```bash
/guild:config init      # scaffold settings.json with all keys + _help block
/guild:config show --sources   # show every resolved key annotated with its source layer
/guild:config validate --effective   # validate the effective resolved config
/guild:config set <key> <value> --scope workspace|project|local   # write one key at a scope
/guild:config providers detect   # probe cross-review providers; print detection table
```

---

## Settings inheritance chain

Guild resolves settings through a **7-source chain** (least to most authoritative):

```
built-in defaults
  < workspace .guild/settings.json
  < workspace .guild/settings.local.json   (gitignored; machine-local overrides)
  < project   .guild/settings.json
  < project   .guild/settings.local.json   (gitignored)
  < --rigor profile expansion
  < CLI flags
```

In a workspace layout (monorepo root with child projects), workspace settings propagate to every child project automatically. A child project that sets only some keys overrides just those keys; the rest inherit from the workspace root. Deep-merge applies to nested blocks — a child that sets `defaults.team.size` does not discard the workspace-level `defaults.quality.budget`.

**Non-inheritable keys.** Two keys have restricted workspace→child propagation:

- `workspace.mode` — workspace detection applies only to the root. A child never inherits the root's workspace classification (unconditional).

# Cost-Aware Model Tiering

Every specialist lane runs on the cheapest model that can handle the work — file reads and summarization on haiku, drafting and reasoning on sonnet, architecture and security review on opus. Guild scores each lane automatically before dispatch and prints the resolved tier so you can see exactly what ran and why.

<Figure src="/diagrams/cost-tiering.svg" alt="Three-tier model diagram: cheap (haiku) for I/O and classification, mid (sonnet) for drafting and reasoning, powerful (opus) for architecture and security" caption="Guild routes each lane to the right tier. You only pay opus rates when the stakes justify it." />

## The three tiers

| Tier | Default model | Typical work |
|---|---|---|
| `cheap` | haiku | File read, tokenize, chunk, summarize, classify, tag — pure I/O, template-guided, low ambiguity |
| `mid` | sonnet | Draft, reason, plan subtasks, single-doc + cross-file relationship extraction — **default task-agent tier** |
| `powerful` | opus | Architecture decisions, security review, graph schema/topology, advisor/critic passes — high-stakes, low frequency |

The tier-to-model map is **host-agnostic**: it lives in `settings.json` under `models.tiers` as `{ cheap, mid, powerful } → { claude, codex, gemini }`. Codex and Gemini slots are `null` by default; adding a new host is a config edit plus an adapter.

## Auto-scoring a lane

For each lane, the orchestrator computes a complexity score from deterministic signals — no LLM call, no guesswork:

| Signal | Score contribution |
|---|---|
| `workType` verb: read/summarize | 0 |
| `workType` verb: draft/extract | +1 |
| `workType` verb: <HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED> | +2 |
| Blast-radius — affected file/module count (each unit ≥1) | + count × `scoreWeights.blastRadius` |
| Upstream `depends-on:` contract present | +1 |
| <HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED> sensitivity flag | +1 |
| Prior-attempt escalation on this lane | +1 (sticky for the run) |

Score bands map to tiers:

| Score | Tier |
|---|---|
| 0 | `cheap` |
| 1–2 | `mid` |
| ≥ 3 | `powerful` |

Score and resolved tier are printed at dispatch. Signal weights are tunable via `models.scoreWeights` in `settings.json`.

## Precedence

```
--model-tier=<tier>   CLI flag           (top — run-level escape hatch)
  > tier: <tier> in plan lane            (per-lane override in .guild/plan/*.md)
    > settings.json models:              (repo config)
      > built-in default                 (cheap-biased tier-map)
```

Use `--model-tier` only as a one-off override. Permanent adjustments belong in `settings.json` or the plan lane. See the [configuration reference](/docs/configuration) for all `models.*` keys.

# v1 → v2 Migration

Guild v2 is a full clean slate: flat command surface, one `--rigor` knob, cost-aware model tiering, and a new lifecycle structure with dedicated phase verbs. This guide documents every removed/renamed command, the config and flag changes, and the new v2 surfaces you'll encounter upgrading from v1.

Start here if you're upgrading. For the complete `settings.json` key reference, see
the [Configuration Reference](/docs/configuration).

---

## TL;DR — the 60-second version

- **`/guild:guild-x` → `/guild:x`** — the `:` plugin namespace stays (Claude Code
  requires it); v2 drops the redundant `guild-` command prefix. The main entry
  command is `/guild:guild [brief]`.
- **Flag soup → `--rigor=quick|standard|deep`** — one knob replaces five tuning flags
  plus 5 global flags and a universal `--dry-run`.
- **New phase subcommands:** `init ideate plan build qa ops`. The Operations verb is `ops`.
- **`/guild:guild-team` is removed** — team-compose is folded into `/guild:plan`.
- **`/guild:guild-diagnose` → `/guild:fix`** — verb rename.
- **Initiatives are new and opt-in** — one-off runs remain first-class.
- **No shims that execute, and no redirect stubs.** Every removed name was deleted in
  v2.0. An unknown subcommand prints usage help only.

# Dashboard

`/guild:dashboard` launches the local benchmark UI against **this project** — every recorded run imported and scored, plus the project's knowledge graph and wiki, browsable in one place. Everything stays on your machine: the server binds to `127.0.0.1`, reads `.guild/` read-only, and nothing phones home.

```
/guild:dashboard
```

## What it does

The command resolves a benchmark checkout, starts its server pointed at your project, imports your recorded runs, and prints the URL:

1. **Resolve the benchmark checkout.** A workspace sibling `benchmark/` directory is used first; if none exists, the launcher falls back to a shallow clone under `.<HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED>` (gitignored) — but only with your explicit approval (see [network posture](#no-network-by-default) below).
2. **Start the server on a free port.** Default port `3055`; if it's bound, the launcher picks a free one. Pass `--port` to pin it. The server is session-scoped — no daemon is left running.
3. **Import your recorded runs.** The launcher bulk-calls the benchmark's existing lifecycle-import API once per `.guild/runs/<run-id>/` that has `logs/v1.4-events.jsonl`. Skip with `--no-import`.
4. **Point the UI at your project.** The server runs with `--project-root` set to your project, which enables the read-only knowledge routes.
5. **Print the URL.** Open it in a browser.

## Usage and flags

```bash
/guild:dashboard                  # resolve, serve, import, print URL
/guild:dashboard --port 4000      # pin the port instead of 3055/free-port
/guild:dashboard --no-import      # skip the bulk run import
/guild:dashboard --install        # permit the clone + npm install network actions
/guild:dashboard --dry-run        # print what would happen; execute nothing
```

| Flag | Effect |
|------|--------|

the receipt protocol never does.

do not add a step-by-step plan section:

<The desired end-state, stated as an outcome — what must be TRUE when this lane is

they must exhibit.>

CONSTRAINTS
<Boundaries and invariants: file-ownership scope (write ONLY these paths), frozen
contracts/schemas that must not change, behavior that must stay byte-identical,
security/closed-key regimes, anything the plan's autonomy-policy forbids.>

<The exact command(s) or check(s) that prove the goal is met — e.g. the test command

pre-existing tests"). The lane must run this itself before writing its receipt.>

FREEDOM
<Method is left open: choose your own decomposition, ordering, and implementation
approach within CONSTRAINTS. If you deviate from any assumption stated in the plan,
or discover the goal is better met another way, do it — and report every such
deviation in the receipt's `notes`/`assumptions` so the lead can audit the path
taken.>
````

# /guild:dashboard — visual dashboard over this project

Launches the benchmark factory's web UI **against the live project**
(`--project-root`): imported runs, the knowledge-graph explorer, and the wiki
browser. Server binds 127.0.0.1 only; project routes are read-only.

Initiative: guild-dashboard (WI-3). Contract pinned in
`.guild/spec/v2-gap-closure.md §"The cross-repo dashboard contract"`.

## Args & local flags

- Args: — (no positional)
- `--port N` — preferred port (default 3055; next free port used when bound).
- `--no-import` — skip the bulk lifecycle import of `.guild/runs/*`.
- `--install` — pre-approve the network leg (git clone / npm ci) when no
  benchmark checkout exists. Without it the launcher prints the exact
  commands and exits (REQUIRED-INSTALL) — it never touches the network.
- `--dry-run` — print the resolved plan (checkout, port, run dirs, serve
  command); execute nothing.

## Gates

- **I** (interactive) on REQUIRED-INSTALL: clone/install is network +
  always-ask class — the skill surfaces the exact commands and asks before
  re-running with `--install`. Everything else is localhost-only and ungated.

## Output

Prints the dashboard URL (`http://127.0.0.1:<port>/`), the imported-run
summary (per-run failures non-fatal), and the server PID + how to stop it
(`kill <pid>` — session-scoped process, no daemon). No `.guild/` data writes
(only `.<HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED>` under a confirmed `--install`).

## Run recording

Before launch, start a lightweight run (SC-B, §435):

```bash
node ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/dist/run-trace.js start \
  --command=/guild:dashboard \
  --run-class=lightweight \
  --cwd "$(pwd)"
```

`run-class=lightweight`: dashboard is a read/serve diagnostic, analogous to
stats. No `--initiative` flag (NN#5).

## Dispatch

Thin entrypoint — no business logic here. Invoke the `guild:dashboard` skill
with `$ARGUMENTS` forwarded. The skill resolves the project root (workspace
root when `.guild/workspace.json` is present), runs
`scripts/dashboard-launch.ts`, handles the REQUIRED-INSTALL confirm gate, and
reports URL + import count. All deterministic work (checkout resolution, port
pick, serve spawn, readiness poll, lifecycle imports) lives in the script.
"}

   **deterministic on-disk signal** (signal→class rules by pointer to
   `lifecycle/lifecycle-overview.md §436`). **No LLM guess** for selection.
2. **No class silently skipped.** A skipped class ⇒ explicit
   `not_applicable: <reason>`. A class applicable but with no harness ⇒
   `gap: <class> applicable but no harness found`. Every one of the five
   classes therefore has an explicit selected / `not_applicable` / `gap`
   disposition with a reason.

   the 3-choice prompt `[proceed] [edit-selection] [explain-signals]`.
   `edit-selection` records `override: user`. There is **no `--classes=` flag**
   — selection is signal-derived then user-overridable, never flag-passed.

   `target-architecture.md §600–606`** — never re-spell the frozen fields.

# v2 Lifecycle

This document is the **single lifecycle truth** for Guild v2. It supersedes
`plugin/guild-plan.md §8` — the v1 7-step linear spine — which is frozen as the
historical v1 record and now carries a `supersedes:` pointer back to this page.
`guild-plan.md` is not deleted; its 8 spine skills are *re-homed* (not deleted)
as the implementation of the Planning and Development phases, and it is the
default forward path, not a peer model.

## Framing

> Guild v2 is **one state machine with six phase entrypoints and three lenses**
> (linear / phase / initiative) — linear (`/guild [brief]` walks
> Ideation → Planning → Development → Quality), phase (`/guild <phase>` jumps to
> any phase with a backward-then-forward prerequisite resolver), and initiative
> (an opt-in wrapper owning cross-phase progress + the close gate).

The shipped v1 7-step spine is re-homed, not deleted: its skills become the
implementation of Planning + Development; it is the default forward path, not a
peer model.

# Edge Cases and Advisory Defaults

This file captures failure modes that should shape v2 implementation and review.

## Backend and tmux

| Edge case | Handling |
|---|---|
| `tmux` missing | Use `subagent`; record fallback in team file. |
| Already inside tmux | Do not launch nested agent-team; tell operator to rerun from a plain shell if agent-team is required. |
| Env var missing | Refuse agent-team launch; use subagent only if the user accepts changed semantics. |
| Agent-team session name collision | Dry-run first, then relaunch with explicit session name. |
| Teammate exits without receipt | `TaskCompleted` hook blocks completion; lane is incomplete. |

## Command Migration (clean-slate break)

| Edge case | Handling |
|---|---|
| User invokes a removed `/guild:guild-*` v1 command | Refuse and point to the exact `/guild:<verb>` replacement and `MIGRATION.md`. The `:` plugin namespace **stays** (Claude Code requires it); v2 dropped only the redundant `guild-` command prefix, and the v1→v2 redirect stubs were deleted in v2.0 (no silent aliasing). |
| User types `/guild ship` (legacy spelling) | Map to `/guild ops` and tell the user the Operations verb is `ops`; do not run silently under the old token. |
| User passes a genuinely removed flag (`--codex-review`, `--restart` as a first word, `--allow-larger`) | Map/print the replacement: `--review={local\|cross\|off}`, `/guild resume --restart`, `--team-size=N`; reference `MIGRATION.md`. **Note:** `--loops`/`--loop-cap`/`--codex-cap` are **not** removed — they are accepted as power-user flags (parsed at the `read-guild-config.ts` arg-parse switch for `--loops`/`--loop-cap`/`--codex-cap`); `--rigor={quick\|standard\|deep}` + `.guild/settings.json` is the recommended path. |
| `/guild [brief]` whose first token collides with a reserved <HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED> token | Treat as that subcommand (reserved set is closed); a quoted/free-text brief is the linear lens. Always surface and gate the detection — never silent. |
| `/guild` reaches an interactive gate in a non-interactive/CI context | Hard-fail with an actionable message ("interactive gate reached in non-interactive context; pass `--auto-approve=…` or name a phase"); never assume autonomy. |

## Initiative Attachment (opt-in)

| Edge case | Handling |
|---|---|
| No durable-goal signal | Default `one_off`; no initiative directory; run lives at `.guild/runs/<run-id>/`. Never auto-attach. |
| Durable-goal signal present | Ask `[new / existing / one-off]` before team-compose; never silently auto-attach. |
